item.title: Synthesis of N -Linked Amino-Hexyl Fluorotryptophan for Enlicitide, Part 1: Route Scouting
item.description:
Abstract
One of the building blocks in the manufacture of the northern macrocycle of enlicitide decanoate is N-linked amino-hexylfluorotryptophan 1. An efficient, scalable, and protecting-group-free synthesis of this key building block is described. Hallmarks of the synthesis include the use of the Delépine reaction to prepare the required alkylating agent and the alkylation of unprotected fluorotryptophan.

item.title: Industrial Quench Method for Triethylsilane, Featuring Process Development and Safety Measures
item.description:
Abstract
Safe process operation is critically important in the manufacture of active pharmaceutical ingredients. We employed an excess of triethylsilane (Et3SiH) as a reducing agent in the production of the dapagliflozin propanediol monohydrate. Although unreacted Et3SiH must be safely treated prior to disposal, no industrial quenching methods for Et3SiH have previously been reported. Accordingly, a safe treatment method using KOH in MeOH was developed. The quench reaction of Et3SiH under basic conditions was found to be exothermic and to evolve hydrogen. Therefore, measures to ensure safe plant-scale operations were required. The heat release profile during the quenching of Et3SiH was quantitatively evaluated. On the basis of these results, the quench reaction was controlled by adjusting the addition rate of KOH in MeOH. To safely vent the generated flammable hydrogen, it was necessary to maintain the oxygen concentration in the reactor headspace below the limiting oxygen concentration by using nitrogen purging. Implementation of these countermeasures successfully enabled the quenching of Et3SiH at the pilot scale.

item.title: Evolution of a Synthetic Strategy toward Highly Substituted Isoindolinone Glutarimide Fragments
item.description:
Abstract
Herein we report the design, development, and evolution of a first-generation synthesis of benzylamine fragment 1·HCl to a second-generation process for 2·HCl en route to highly substituted isoindolinone glutarimide degrader molecules. Salient features of the two syntheses include directed ortho-metalation of substituted benzoic acids, highly regioselective aromatic halogenations, and divergent strategies to install the key aminomethyl motif. The second-generation, stereoselective-enabling process improves on the first-generation route by transitioning from unreliable reactions to robust transformations and proceeding through isolable solid intermediates, thereby enabling improved impurity control.

item.title: Synthesis of N -Linked Amino-Hexyl Fluorotryptophan for Enlicitide, Part 2: Process Improvements toward Commercial Manufacture
item.description:
Abstract
Herein, we report the development of a robust manufacturing process for N-linked amino-hexyl fluorotryptophan 3, a key building block for enlicitide decanoate (MK-0616), which is an orally bioavailable inhibitor of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9). Targeted process development enabled safe operation of the Delépine reaction, increased yields for the hexamine hydrolysis and enzymatic tryptophan synthesis, and established a robust and selective N-alkylation of 5-fluorotryptophan. Collectively, these improvements afforded the target product with high yield, >98.5% purity, and favorable physical properties suitable for commercial manufacture.

item.title: Technical Note: A Facile and Scalable Synthesis of Versatile Trithiocarbonate Chain Transfer Agents for RAFT Polymerization
item.description:
Abstract
Reversible addition–fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) polymerization is a key tool in modern macromolecular design. Central to its success is the availability of versatile chain transfer agents (CTAs), typically based on thiocarbonylthio compounds. Herein, we report a refined, scalable, and high-yield synthesis of a family of trithiocarbonate RAFT agents based on a propanoic acid leaving group, mimicking the propagating radical of acrylic acid, which permits efficient mediation of the polymerization of a wide range of monomers. We report the synthesis of 2-{[(butylsulfanyl)carbonothioyl]sulfanyl}propanoic acid (BPTC), commonly known as (Propanoic Acid)yl Butyl TrithioCarbonate (PABTC), a highly oil-soluble derivative, 2-{[(dodecylsulfanyl)carbonothioyl]sulfanyl}propanoic acid (DoPAT), and a highly water-soluble derivative, 3-[[[(1-carboxyethyl)thio]carbonothioyl]thio]propanoic acid (CETCP). By optimizing the aqueous-based reaction conditions, we achieved yields of 80% or higher of high-purity products across all three derivatives on a tens of grams scale, without the necessity of intensive organic solvent extraction or multiple recrystallization steps.

item.title: Technical Note: A Practical and Scalable Method for the Preparation of 3-Acylindole Scaffold Using N , N -Dimethylamides via the Vilsmeier–Haack Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
Efficient and scalable methods for the C3 acylation of 2-arylindoles remain limited despite the importance of 3-acyl-2-arylindoles as versatile intermediates in medicinal and synthetic chemistry. Herein, a practical Vilsmeier–Haack acylation protocol employing readily available N,N-dialkylamides and phosphorus oxychloride is described. Systematic reaction optimization identified conditions that provide highly regioselective C3 acylation across a broad range of 2-arylindoles and acylating agents, affording the corresponding products in high isolated yields without chromatographic purification. The operational simplicity of the method, together with its broad functional-group tolerance and gram-scale applicability, makes it a practical alternative to conventional acylation protocols. The synthetic utility of the resulting 3-acyl-2-arylindoles was demonstrated by concise syntheses of representative fused indole heterocycles related to biologically active alkaloids, including fluorescent indoloquinoline, indoloisoquinoline, and carbazole derivatives.

item.title: Process Optimization of a Noyori Transfer Hydrogenation Utilizing a Quality-by-Design Approach: Development of a Robust Step in the Synthesis of Casdatifan
item.description:
Abstract
A key step in the manufacture of casdatifan involves a Noyori transfer hydrogenation of a stereochemically complex difluorodiketone 4 that establishes three contiguous stereocenters in a single transformation. Herein, we describe a systematic quality-by-design (QbD)-driven optimization of this reaction, involving risk assessment to identify critical process parameters, multivariate design of experiments to evaluate their effects, and targeted one-variable-at-a-time (OVAT) studies to further refine operating conditions. Implementation of the optimized, buffer-free conditions resulted in a robust process delivering 74–75% isolated yield with >99% high-performance liquid chromatography purity.

item.title: Operationally Simple Amidation in Isopropanol Using Diphenylphosphinic Chloride
item.description:
Abstract
Described is the coupling of carboxylic acids with amines in isopropanol, followed by the direct isolation of amide products from the reaction mixture. Phosphorus-based reagents were found to be uniquely capable of mediating productive amidation, with diphenylphosphinic chloride (DPPCl) specifically providing the greatest advantage. After reaction completion, direct isolation of desired products can be accomplished by addition of water, where DPPCl reagent byproducts are purged in the filtrate. This experimentally simple all-in reaction and direct isolation protocol was demonstrated across functionally diverse examples and provides a streamlined amidation option when products can be isolated from aqueous isopropanol.

item.title: Evaluation of Potential Second-Generation Manufacturing Routes to Palbociclib
item.description:
Abstract
A potential next-generation manufacturing route to Palbociclib was developed to reduce step count and cycle time relative to the first-generation commercial process while improving overall process sustainability. The final tert-butoxycarbonyl (Boc) deprotection step from the original route was retained to preserve established late-stage impurity clearance and API attributes. The revised synthesis is based on the preparation of a common chloropyridone intermediate (8a) from a readily crystallized hydroxy-pyridone precursor (9), followed by a convergent late-stage C–N bond formation between two advanced heterocyclic fragments. Several coupling approaches, including nucleophilic aromatic substitution and palladium-catalyzed Buchwald–Hartwig amination, were evaluated. High-Throughput Experimentation combined with Design-of-Experiments studies identified a homogeneous palladium-catalyzed amination as the preferred manufacturing solution. Isolation of the coupling product (20) was achieved by reactive crystallization, enabling direct preparation of the advanced intermediate in high purity. Final Boc cleavage with formic acid, followed by basification, afforded palbociclib in high yield and purity. Overall, the route provides a shorter and operationally streamlined manufacturing process, enabling a two-step synthesis of palbociclib (1) from key starting materials 10e and 3b.

item.title: Optimization of a Biocatalytic Asymmetric Sulfur Oxidation Featuring a Protease Workup to Prepare a Key Intermediate in the Manufacture of Ceralasertib
item.description:
Abstract
This study reports the development of an optimized biocatalytic asymmetric sulfur oxidation using a BVMO enzyme to produce a key ceralasertib intermediate. A design of experiments (DoE) approach established a robust operating window that reduced enzyme loading, improved reaction performance, and defined failure mode boundaries. A novel subtilisin-based protease workup was introduced, eliminating emulsions, simplifying liquid–liquid extraction, and enabling rapid, scalable removal of protein residues. Improvements to distillation and crystallization further enhanced process efficiency and manufacturability. Together, these advancements deliver a streamlined, high-yielding, and scalable process suitable for commercial production.

item.title: Enhanced Scale-Up of Rotor-Stator Wet Milling Using Population Balance Modeling with a Novel Exponential Shear-Activated Kernel
item.description:
Abstract
Wet milling is a critical operation in drug substance manufacturing, enabling control of the particle size distribution of active pharmaceutical ingredients. Scaling up of the wet milling process usually involves equipment change. Due to material availability limitations during the early stage of development, there is a limited opportunity to experimentally determine optimal operating conditions for scale-up equipment. As a result, model-based approaches are essential for a reliable transition from the laboratory to commercial production. Existing population balance modeling (PBM) frameworks have enabled model-aided scale-up but typically employ empirical linear relationships between the breakage rate and the shear number, limiting their mechanistic interpretability and cross-scale robustness. This study presents an enhanced PBM kernel formulation that introduces an exponential dependence of the breakage rate on the shear number, reflecting a stress-activated mechanism analogous to barrier-crossing kinetics observed in material deformation and fracture. The proposed kernel retains the structure of the conventional PBM while embedding physical meaning into the shear dependence. Using experimental data from laboratory- and pilot-scale wet mills, the model successfully predicts clinical-scale performance without empirical refitting, demonstrating improved predictive capability. The exponential shear-activated formulation strengthens the physical foundation of the PBM-based scale-up and provides a more generalizable framework for wet milling process design. In addition, a model credibility and regulatory validation framework is proposed to support the regulatory acceptance of model-based digital design approaches for pharmaceutical manufacturing processes.

item.title: Practical Scale-Up of Trickle Bed Continuous Hydrogenation for Pharmaceuticals
item.description:
Abstract
There is a growing trend in the pharmaceutical industry toward the adoption of continuous processing for the synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and intermediates. This enables access to novel synthetic routes by operating at high temperatures and high pressures. Hydrogenation is a key transformation that particularly benefits from continuous processing, offering enhanced volumetric productivity and improved safety profiles. This study presents the development and scale-up of a continuous hydrogenation process, progressing from bench scale to pilot plant operation while addressing challenges associated with material limitations. The scale-up achieved a production rate of 12 kg/day for a pharmaceutical intermediate, with online HPLC employed for real-time process monitoring at both scales. Additionally, this work offers a strategic framework for catalyst selection in continuous hydrogenation and provides a scale-up methodology that can be readily applied when material constraints are present in pharmaceutical manufacturing.

item.title: Toward Chromatography-Free Convergent Peptide Synthesis via Nanostar Sieving
item.description:
Abstract
Liquid-phase peptide synthesis (LPPS) has emerged as a versatile and efficient method for assembling peptides, offering significant advantages in purity and yield. In this study, we investigate the application of organic solvent nanofiltration (OSN) technology in LPPS for peptide fragment assembly by Nanostar Sieving. We report how a nanostar support decorated with solubilizing polymers can be used to achieve solubility at concentrations of up to 40 mM of a 39-mer peptide. This is assembled from eight peptide fragments on an 8-arm, 20 kDa nanostar support. OSN enables effective removal of reagents, byproducts, and unreacted fragments after each coupling cycle, enhancing synthesis efficiency. A photolabile linker was incorporated into the support before fragment assembly, enabling periodic analysis without full global deprotection. The Rink amide linker facilitated the final cleavage of the synthesized peptide using standard global deprotection protocols. Following synthesis, OSN was employed to isolate the peptide from the support. In contrast to previous OSN-assisted peptide fragment assembly methods, which required chromatographic purification to remove unreacted fragments at the end of synthesis, nanostar sieving enables their removal during synthesis. The potential to eliminate the need for chromatography could lead to more efficient and scalable therapeutic peptide production.
